title: Civil War Battlefields

sheetTitle.es: Campos de batalla de la Guerra Civil

summary: See how the United States was divided by 1863, compare the railroads of the North and the South, and find where the war's battles were fought.
subject: History
alsoFits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

image.alt: Preview of the Civil War Battlefields map

layers.name: U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863)
layers.shows: States and territories in 1863 in five legend groups: Union free states; Union slave states (border states); slave states that seceded before Fort Sumter, April 1861; slave states that seceded after Fort Sumter; and territories. State names are labeled on the map. No pop-up.
layers.source: State boundaries from IPUMS NHGIS, grouped by the MapMaker team

layers.name: Civil War Battlefield Boundary
layers.shows: The land each battle covered, as tan shaded areas. Each pop-up gives the battle's name, its size in acres and the state (two-letter code).
layers.source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program

layers.name: Civil War Core Areas
layers.shows: The core of each battlefield, where the heaviest fighting took place, as striped areas. Same pop-up as the boundaries.
layers.source: National Park Service, American Battlefield Protection Program

layers.name: Boundary between Union and Confederacy
layers.shows: The line between the Union and the Confederacy. No pop-up.
layers.source: Not stated on the layer (hosted by the MapMaker team)

layers.name: Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static)
layers.source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team

layers.name: Civil War Battlefields
layers.shows: Battle locations as diamonds colored by result (Union victory, Confederate victory, Inconclusive) and sized by casualties; gray circles are battles with no result recorded (Other). Each pop-up gives the battle's name and dates and a picture; it does not give the result. The diamonds disappear when you zoom in very close.

knownIssues.note: Uses the same text as the boundary layer, so it calls the core area "the battlefield area".

The layer item's legend labels are inverted: Union victories are drawn with the symbol the legend calls "Confederate Victory", and Confederate victories with the "Union Victory" symbol (for example Gettysburg shows as a Confederate victory). The MapMaker team is correcting the item. No question in this lesson depends on the result of a battle.
The American Battlefield Trust image in the battle pop-ups does not load; the name and dates still show.

compellingQuestion.en: How did the geography of a divided nation shape the Civil War, as the map shows the country in 1863?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Cómo influyó la geografía de una nación dividida en la Guerra Civil, tal como el mapa muestra el país en 1863?

questions.task: Use the legend for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) to sort the states: which seceded before Fort Sumter, which after, and which slave states stayed in the Union? Then spot the state on this 1863 layer that did not exist in 1861 (West Virginia), as the way in to how the map's date matters.
frontOfClass: Open the legend and show the five groups for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863).
Point to South Carolina and match its shade to its legend group.
Point to Virginia and match its shade.
Point to Kentucky and match its shade.
Ask: which states left before Fort Sumter, which after, and which slave states stayed in the Union?
Ask: the layer shows 1863; which state on it did not exist in 1861?

steps.en: Open the legend and find the groups for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863).
steps.es: Abre la leyenda y busca los grupos de la capa U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) (estados y territorios de la Guerra Civil de EE. UU.).

steps.en: Match each state's shade to its group.
steps.es: Relaciona el tono de cada estado con su grupo.

steps.en: Find the state on the map that did not exist in 1861 (the layer shows the country in 1863).
steps.es: Busca el estado del mapa que no existía en 1861 (la capa muestra el país en 1863).

ask.en: Which states left the Union before the attack on Fort Sumter in April 1861? Which left after? Which slave states stayed in the Union? Which state on the map did not exist in 1861?
ask.es: ¿Qué estados dejaron la Unión antes del ataque al fuerte Sumter en abril de 1861? ¿Cuáles se fueron después? ¿Qué estados esclavistas se quedaron en la Unión? ¿Qué estado del mapa no existía en 1861?

answer.where: Legend for U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863): the groups are Union Free State, Union slave state (border state), Slave state seceding before Fort Sumter, April 1861, Slave state seceding after Fort Sumter, April 1861, and Territories. State names are labels on the layer; zoom in if a label is hidden. Counts from the layer: 7 before, 4 after, 5 border states. West Virginia (admitted June 20, 1863) is the state that did not exist in 1861; in 1861 its counties were part of Virginia, which seceded.

answer.text: West Virginia split from Virginia and joined the Union as a state in June 1863, which is why it appears on this 1863 map. The two Union shades are close (dark blue and lighter blue), so students may need the legend side by side with the map.

questions.task: Zoom to Washington, D.C. Which two states border it? Using the legend shades of those two states, what would have happened to the capital if Maryland had left the Union?
frontOfClass: Zoom in to Washington, D.C., between Maryland and Virginia.
Point to the white dashed Boundary between Union and Confederacy running past the capital.
Open the legend and check Maryland's shade, then Virginia's.
Ask: which two states border the capital, and which side was each on?
Ask: what would have happened to Washington if Maryland had left the Union?

steps.en: Zoom in to Washington, D.C., on the east coast between Maryland and Virginia.
steps.es: Acércate a Washington D. C., en la costa este, entre Maryland y Virginia.

steps.en: Find the two states that border it.
steps.es: Busca los dos estados que lo rodean.

steps.en: Check each one's shade in the legend.
steps.es: Comprueba el tono de cada uno en la leyenda.

ask.en: Which two states border Washington, D.C.? What would have happened to the capital if Maryland had left the Union?
ask.es: ¿Qué dos estados rodean Washington D. C.? ¿Qué le habría pasado a la capital si Maryland hubiera dejado la Unión?

answer.where: Zoom to the District of Columbia (a small unshaded area labeled on the States layer). Its neighbors are Maryland (legend: Union slave state, border state) and Virginia (legend: Slave state seceding after Fort Sumter). The white dashed Boundary between Union and Confederacy runs right past the capital.
answer.accept: Maryland and Virginia. A good answer uses the legend to say Virginia had seceded, so if Maryland had left too, Washington would have been surrounded by Confederate states and cut off from the rest of the Union.

questions.task: Compare the Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static) layer (thin dark gray lines) north and south of the Boundary between Union and Confederacy (a white dashed line). Turning the States layer off in Map layers makes the lines easier to see. Which side had more railroads, and why would that matter in a war?
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn off U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863).
Point to the thin dark gray lines of Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static).
Follow the white dashed Boundary between Union and Confederacy from the Atlantic to the Mississippi.
Ask: which side has more railroad lines?
Ask: why would railroads matter in a war?
Turn U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) back on.

steps.en: Find the white dashed boundary between the Union and the Confederacy.
steps.es: Busca la línea blanca discontinua que marca la frontera entre la Unión y la Confederación.

steps.en: In Map layers, turn U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) off to see the railroad lines better.
steps.es: En las capas del mapa (Map layers), desactiva la capa U.S. Civil War States and Territories (1863) para ver mejor las líneas de ferrocarril.

steps.en: Compare the railroads (thin dark gray lines) north and south of the boundary.
steps.es: Compara los ferrocarriles (líneas finas de color gris oscuro) al norte y al sur de la frontera.

ask.en: Which side had more railroads? Why would railroads matter in a war?
ask.es: ¿Qué lado tenía más ferrocarriles? ¿Por qué importaban los ferrocarriles en una guerra?

answer.where: Railroads 1826 to 1863 (static) layer and the Boundary between Union and Confederacy line (legend: white dashed). The lines are visibly denser north of the boundary, above all between the Mississippi River and the Atlantic coast. The map shows lines, not mileage.
answer.accept: The North (Union side). A good answer says a denser network let the Union move soldiers, food and weapons faster and farther, keep armies supplied, and shift troops between fronts; the South had fewer lines and gaps between them.

questions.task: Zoom to Virginia, then to Maryland and Pennsylvania, and click the tan battlefield areas for names, sizes and state. Where were most battles fought, and which were fought in Union states (check the state's shade in the legend)?
frontOfClass: Zoom to Virginia and point to the tan battlefield areas between Washington and Richmond.
Click one tan area and read the battle's name, acres and state.
Zoom to Maryland and Pennsylvania and click the tan area at Gettysburg.
Open the legend and check Pennsylvania's shade.
Ask: where were most battles fought?
Ask: which battles were fought in a Union state?

steps.en: Zoom to Virginia, then to Maryland and Pennsylvania.
steps.es: Acércate a Virginia y luego a Maryland y Pensilvania.

steps.en: Click the tan shaded areas of two battlefields and read their names.
steps.es: Haz clic en las zonas color canela de dos campos de batalla y lee sus nombres.

steps.en: Use the legend to find a battlefield in a Union state.
steps.es: Usa la leyenda para encontrar un campo de batalla en un estado de la Unión.

ask.en: Where were most battles fought? Name a battle fought in a state the legend shows as a Union state.
ask.es: ¿Dónde se libraron la mayoría de las batallas? Nombra una batalla librada en un estado que la leyenda muestre como estado de la Unión.

answer.where: Civil War Battlefield Boundary pop-ups: the title is the battle name; Battlefield Acres and State Name (two-letter code) are listed below. Most tan areas are in Virginia (the layer has far more in VA than in any other state). Union states by the legend: Maryland (border state) has Antietam (34,937 acres), South Mountain, Monocacy, Boonsboro, Williamsport, Hancock and Folck's Mill; Pennsylvania (Union free state) has Gettysburg (73,551 acres) and Hanover. If a pop-up says 1 of 2, a core area sits under the boundary; use the arrows.
answer.accept: Most battles were in the Confederate states, above all Virginia, between the two capitals. Any battle named from a Maryland or Pennsylvania pop-up, most often Antietam or Gettysburg.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, a sketch of the front line with notes (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

student.en: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.
student.es: Responde la pregunta central con evidencia de al menos dos capas del mapa. Puedes escribir un párrafo, dibujar en el mapa o hacer ambas cosas.

objectives: Sort the states on the 1863 map into those that seceded before Fort Sumter, those that seceded after, and the slave states that stayed in the Union, using the legend, and notice that the layer shows 1863, so West Virginia appears as a Union state that did not exist in 1861.
Locate Washington, D.C., identify the two states that border it, and explain from their legend shades why Maryland staying in the Union mattered.
Compare the density of railroads north and south of the Boundary between Union and Confederacy and say why that difference mattered in a war.
Find battlefields in Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania, read their names and sizes from the pop-ups, and identify which were fought in Union states.
Use evidence from at least two layers to explain how the geography of a divided nation shaped the Civil War.
discussion: Most of the tan battlefield areas sit in Virginia, between Washington and Richmond. What about the map explains why so much of the fighting happened there?
You compared railroad lines north and south of the boundary. What else, not shown on this map, would you want to know before deciding how big the Union's advantage really was?

Antietam and Gettysburg are the biggest battlefield areas in Union states. Why might a Confederate army have crossed the boundary into Maryland and Pennsylvania, given what the map shows about the two sides?

differentiation.support: Do question 1 together from the front with the legend open beside the map, and write the five group names on the board with one state each.
differentiation.stretch: Click the largest diamonds in Civil War Battlefields to read their names and dates, and ask whether the biggest battles lie near the boundary, on railroads, or both.

resources.title: Defining Battles of the Civil War

beforeYouStart.en: In November 1860, Abraham Lincoln was elected president. He opposed the spread of slavery into the western territories, and Southern slave states began to leave the Union to form the Confederate States of America. In April 1861, Confederate forces attacked Fort Sumter, a Union fort in South Carolina, and the Civil War began.
beforeYouStart.es: En noviembre de 1860, Abraham Lincoln fue elegido presidente. Se oponía a que la esclavitud se extendiera a los territorios del Oeste, y los estados esclavistas del Sur comenzaron a separarse de la Unión para formar los Estados Confederados de América. En abril de 1861, fuerzas confederadas atacaron Fort Sumter, un fuerte de la Unión en Carolina del Sur, y comenzó la Guerra Civil.

readingTheMap.en: States are shaded by side in 1863: shades of blue for the Union and shades of brown for the Confederacy; open the legend to see which shade means which group. State names are written on the map. A white dashed line marks the boundary between the two sides. Thin dark gray lines are railroads built by 1863. Diamonds mark battles, colored by who won: use the legend to read the result, because a battle's pop-up gives its name and dates but not the result. White diamonds are Inconclusive and gray circles are Other. Bigger diamonds mean more soldiers were killed, wounded, captured or missing. Tan shaded areas show the land each battlefield covered, and areas with diagonal stripes show where the fighting was heaviest.
readingTheMap.es: Los estados aparecen sombreados según su bando en 1863: tonos azules para la Unión y tonos marrones para la Confederación; abre la leyenda para ver qué tono corresponde a cada grupo. Los nombres de los estados están escritos en el mapa. Una línea blanca discontinua marca la frontera entre los dos bandos. Las líneas finas de color gris oscuro son los ferrocarriles construidos hasta 1863. Los rombos marcan las batallas, con un color según quién ganó: usa la leyenda para saber el resultado, porque la ventana emergente de una batalla da su nombre y sus fechas, pero no el resultado. Los rombos blancos son batallas sin vencedor claro (Inconclusive) y los círculos grises son otras (Other). Los rombos más grandes indican más soldados muertos, heridos, capturados o desaparecidos. Las zonas color canela muestran el terreno que ocupó cada campo de batalla, y las zonas con rayas diagonales muestran dónde la lucha fue más intensa.

reflection.en: What did the map show you about the Civil War that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
reflection.es: ¿Qué te mostró el mapa sobre la Guerra Civil que quizá no habrías notado solo con la lectura?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: Every layer is on when the map opens and there are no bookmarks, so students zoom to Virginia, Washington, D.C., Maryland and Pennsylvania themselves. Battle pop-ups give the name and dates; the result is read from the legend.

misconceptions.claim: All slave states joined the Confederacy.
misconceptions.response: The legend shows five slave states that stayed in the Union: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri and West Virginia.

misconceptions.claim: The war was fought evenly across the North and the South.
misconceptions.response: Most battlefields on the map are in Confederate states, above all Virginia.

standards.text: Identify the division (Confederate and Union States, Border states, western territories) of the United States at the outbreak of the Civil War
Locate places and regions directly related to major eras and turning points in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
Analyze the effects of physical and human geographic factors such as weather, landforms, waterways, transportation, and communication on major historical events in the United States
Use maps, satellite images, photographs, and other representations to explain relationships between the locations of places and regions, and changes in their environmental characteristics
Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
